- When sentiment is low (≤0.3) and forecast spikes upward, reduce the forecast peak to avoid overreaction.  
- If recent history shows strong mean reversion (prices trending back toward prior 5-10 day average), dampen forecast momentum.  
- When sentiment is high (≥0.7) and forecast is below recent highs, adjust upward to reflect bullish sentiment.  
- Avoid forecasting sharp upward moves after a recent dip unless sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.6) and price has not yet rebounded.  
- If forecast consistently overshoots true outcome by >5% in the first 5-7 days of the horizon, reduce early forecast values.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows a strong upward trend after a low, model should not over-predict early in the horizon — delay peak until later days.  
- When sentiment is volatile (fluctuating between 0.2–0.8), avoid averaging or smoothing forecasts — use sentiment as a weight to adjust forecast direction.  
- If sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.2) and forecast is rising, reduce forecast slope to avoid false optimism.  
- For long horizons (e.g., 30d), if true outcome shows a late surge (last 5–7 days), model should not over-forecast early — adjust forecast to lag slightly behind true trend.
